The faith and dharma of the Distinct Teaching take the correct as their essence.
The faith and dharma of the Perfect Teaching likewise take the correct as their essence.

If one discusses the practices horizontally, these are the various *pāramitās*, as well as loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; one should then teach the essence of these practices.
If both the horizontal and vertical dimensions of all practices possess an essence, then the foundation is established and the Way arises.
If the essence possesses practice, then the essence is manifested by means of that practice.
To further clarify the circular and vertical practice: from the five stages (*pañca-varga*) and the six faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), similarity is taken as the essence;
from the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) up to Equal Enlightenment (*samābodhi*), the true reality itself is used as the essence.
Regarding "transversal practice," as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
"All dharmas are the Mahāyāna; because they are unobtainable, and because they are unobtainable, they are the true reality (*bhūtanimitta*)."
This text states:
"Not apprehending any dharmas, whether existent or non-existent," and "bestowing upon each of his sons equally one great chariot"—this is precisely its meaning.
When the youth Mañjuśrī saw Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and realized that conditioned existence possesses a true essence.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"Giving without abiding in signs is like a person with eyes who sees various forms."
This is also its meaning. When it moves vertically, it has a certain substance, and thus the carriage is high;
when it moves horizontally, it has a certain substance, and thus the carriage is broad.
The lofty and vast momentum proceeds with even and upright steps, as swift as the wind, and so forth.

Second, regarding those who practice according to the sūtras: the two preceding practices of faith and dharma involve a broad scope of mental engagement over time, potentially lasting for many kalpas, like a long-encircling net.
If one practices according to the specific ritual methods detailed in various sutras, fixing the date and time, it is like a harsh assault.
If one practices according to the circumstances of the event, the practice lacks substance.

If one practices according to the principle, causing this wisdom of emptiness to correspond with the practice, one can shatter immeasurable obstacles and transgressions that hinder the Path and attain the patience of non-arising; only then does this practice possess substance.
The various distinct practices found in the sutras are numerous; briefly stated, there are four:
namely, the practice of constant walking, the practice of constant sitting, the practice of half-walking and half-sitting, and the practice of neither walking nor sitting.

All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) each have their own objective characteristics and methods; though they involve diligent physical exertion and ascetic discipline, they all take the correct contemplation of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa-samyagdarśana*) as their essence.
Moment after moment, without interruption, they are pure like space. A detailed exposition of the intent of this contemplation is as explained in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Mohe zhiguan).

However, the Vinaya-piṭaka of the Hīnayāna does not permit the repentance of grave offenses (*ānantarya*). The Sūtra-piṭaka, for those who have committed such grave offenses, instructs them to contemplate the Buddha-body; yet this "Buddha-body" is the contemplation of emptiness.
Furthermore, while it contains methods such as the Constant Practice (*nitya-caryā*), it takes partial emptiness as its fundamental essence.
The Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) also clarifies methods such as constant practice, yet it takes "immediate emptiness" as its essence.

The Distinct Teaching (Biejiao) involves sequential progression, while the Perfect Teaching (Yuanxing) is empty and harmonious; both, however, take the true reality-mark (zheng shixiang) as their essence.
By means of these four practices traversing the five flavors, the essence of the methods can be understood through logical inference. Third, regarding the coarse and the subtle:

in the *Zang* (Tripitaka) and *Tong* (Shared) vehicles, the faith-based and dharma-based truths are like horizontal and vertical practices; because they take the provisional semblance of the true reality (*dharmatā*) as their essence, both their essence and their practice are coarse.

Distinctly, the faith in the Dharma is true, while the various practices appear to be either horizontal or vertical; although they rely on different gates, they take the correct and ultimate reality as their essence. Because the cause is impermanent, the fruit is eternal; thus, while the practices are coarse, the essence is subtle and wondrous.
The Perfect [Teaching]—the faith and the reality of the Dharma—is like the horizontal and vertical; it is the true essence of the Perfect Gate, wherein both essence and practice are sublime.
One may understand the distinctions between the coarse and the sublime by examining them throughout the five flavors, and so forth.
If one practices the "equal practices" according to the methods of various sutras, taking the collateral [practices] as the essence, then both the essence and the practice are coarse;
if one takes the primary [practice] as the essence, then the practice is coarse while the essence is subtle.
The excellence of both its essence and its practice can be understood by analogy with what precedes.
The same applies to the progression through the five flavors, as has been explained at length.

Fourth, regarding the "opening of the coarse": this refers to opening up the two practices of faith and dharma within the Tripiṭaka, which is the definitive resolution of the Śrāvaka teachings and is the king among all sūtras.
Having heard [the teaching], one contemplates it with earnest attention and thereby draws near to the unsurpassed path.

Hearing and immediately practicing with faith is "practice through hearing" (śrutamayī-pratipatti), while contemplating is "practice through reflection" (cintāmayī-pratipatti); both of these draw one near to the unsurpassed path, which is the signless practice (animitta-caryā) of the Mahāyāna and brings one close to the Truth.
Even those who practice the horizontal path—those who bow their heads, raise their hands, sing hymns, or scatter their minds—all have already attained the Buddha-way.

Since even the most superficial level of the Tripitaka is revealed as wondrous, how much more so for the Shared, Distinct, and Perfect teachings, which can be understood through the power of one's own insight.

Regarding the opening of the discussion on the methods of constant practice according to the Hīnayāna and so forth: even the slightest and most minute good deeds, there is not one that does not lead to Buddhahood; this can be understood through reflection, and so forth.
